title: Revealing the genetic architectures underlying organ-specific aging based on proteomic data

paper_content.abstract: Organ-specific plasma protein signatures identified via proteomic profiling could be used to quantitatively track organ aging. However, the genetic determinants and molecular mechanisms underlying the organ-specific aging process remain poorly characterized. Here we integrated large-scale plasma proteomic and genomic data from 51,936 UK Biobank participants to uncover the genetic architectures underlying aging across 13 organs. We identified 119 genetic loci associated with organ aging, including 27 shared across multiple organs, and prioritized 554 risk genes involved in organ-relevant biological pathways, such as T cell–mediated immunity in immune aging. Causal inference analyses indicated that accelerated heart and muscle aging increase the risk of heart failure, whereas kidney aging contributes to hypertension. Moreover, smoking initiation was positively linked to the aging of the lung, intestine, kidney, and stomach. These findings establish a genetic foundation for understanding organ-specific aging and provide insights for promoting healthy longevity.
paper_content.introduction:
Biological aging refers to the gradual and cumulative changes in the biological functions of an organism as time advances1. These changes lead to a decline in physiological capabilities and an increase in disease susceptibility2,3. Investigating the underlying mechanisms of biological aging can enhance our comprehension of the processes contributing to aging-related diseases, thereby informing the development of potential therapeutic interventions.

Most of studies on biological aging focus on whole-body aging indicators, such as healthspan4, lifespan5,6 and longevity7. Given the distinct characteristics of various organs, organ aging, which refers to the biological aging specific to particular organ systems, has increasingly become a research hotspot8–10. Several methods have been established for assessing organ aging. For example, some studies11,12 used MRI-based brain volume and functional connectivity measurements to measure brain aging, but MRI measurements are costly and do not provide molecular insights. Some other studies have used clinical chemistry markers to measure organ aging8,13,14. However, many of these markers have low organ specificity, making them difficult to interpret for organ-specific aging. Moreover, suitable and easily measurable clinical chemistry markers are not yet available for some organs (e.g., intestine and stomach). Therefore, we need to find other indicators for organ aging.

Proteins are the final products of gene expression and the principal functional constituents of cellular and biological processes. Moreover, most drug targets and biomarkers are proteins15,16. In clinical practice, certain plasma proteins have been used to noninvasively evaluate the health status of specific organs, such as alanine transaminase for liver damage17,18. Therefore, finding organ-specific proteins in plasma could track human organ aging. Indeed, recent studies successfully used plasma proteomics data to predict organ aging9,19,20. However, these studies primarily focused on identifying correlations between aging and other phenotypes, without delving into the underlying genetic determinants of organ aging. Moreover, causal associations between organ aging and diseases were not explored.

In this study, using plasma proteomics data from the UK Biobank PharmaProteomics Project (UKB-PPP)21, we trained models to predict organ aging for 13 human organs. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) was then performed to pinpoint the genomic loci associated with organ aging. Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was further used to explore the causal relationship between aging-related diseases, modifiable lifestyle factors and organ aging. Our results could enhance the comprehension of the genetic basis of organ aging and highlighted the causal relationship between organ aging and other traits.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this study, the authors constructed models to predict organ-specific aging using proteomics data, and conducted a thorough investigation searching for genetic determinants of organ-specific aging in large populations. Extensive functional annotations were performed to explore effector genes of the identified loci. They also construct polygenic risk scores to assess associations with aging-related diseases for clinical implications. This study is well designed and provides very interesting results of genetic architectures for organ aging, which provide new insights into the understanding of the aging process and facilitate the discovery of anti-aging interventions. The methodology are sound to support the conclusions. The manuscript is well-written. Overall, this is a very nice piece of work, which deserves to be published. I have only a few minor points to potentially improve this work.
Comments:
1. The authors looked up whether the significant loci associated with corresponding organ-associated phenotypes in previous GWAS studies. It would be better to check the previous association results for phenotypes related to other organs, since "no organ system is an island".
2. When comparing with previous GWASs, the authors should present the results of overlapping findings.
3. Methods: The authors should provide the weights of proteins in each model to help readers understand the importance or contribution of each protein in the model’s predictions.
4. Specify the method used to assess the relationship between delta ages and diseases, which should be explicitly described in the text.
5. The authors should make the GWAS summary data publicly available.
6. In line 277, "supplementary Table 17" should be corrected to "supplementary Table 16".
7. The X-axis title is missing in Figure 5A.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Zhu and colleagues used Olink plasma proteomics data from the UK Biobank to study the genetic architecture of the multi-organ proteomics age derived from machine learning models. Proteomics age has been an increasingly used biomarker in aging research. The authors used three different machine-learning models to derive the organ-specific age. Then, they used the Z-scores aging biomarkers as phenotypes to run a GWAS and several post-GWAS analyses. The authors made a great effort to analyze the data extensively. The topic is needed in a timely manner and may provide additional insights on previous research endeavors. However, the rigor and interpretation of these results need to be further scrutinized. Below are some of my concerns and comments.
1) Writing: Overall, the writing and flow of the current paper need improvement. Especially for the Abstract, the main messages are obscure, and it seems more like a Method section, not a highlight of the critical findings in this study. For example, the authors state: "Furthermore, we construct polygenic risk scores to assess their association with aging-related diseases. Subsequent Mendelian randomization analysis revealed the potential causal effects of organ aging on disease risk status". I don't think these are the main messages. Instead, they are the specific methods and analyses the authors used in this study. Similarly, for the rest of the manuscript, a clear flow should guide the organization of the writing, including the intuition for the genetic analyses you chose to run.
2) ML model for age prediction: Regarding the age prediction model, the authors should carefully scrutinize the model's overfitting/generalizability with the ML models you employed on the proteomics data. In the previous papers (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06802-1; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03164-7), the authors found evident model overfitting and used feature selection or regularization terms to battle this phenomenon. In the current writing, the author only showed the Pearson's r between the predicted age and chronological age in Supplementary eFigure S2 (not sure whether this is for test data and the training or the entire population). The authors should report Pearson's r and other loss metrics for the training/validation/test results to show no severe overfitting. In S Fig. 3, the authors associated the chronological age with the delta age and showed no significant associations. This is very surprising, as age bias (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2213158223000086) is very common in any age prediction model. In addition, why did the author use logistic regression to associate two quantitative variables?
3) Genetics: For GWAS, the QC'ed number of valid SNPs (13206758) is much larger than that of the previous GWAS, using imputed data from the UK Biobank. Can authors state the discrepancy?
See some references from previous UKBB GWAS:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0571-7#Sec8
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17368-1?fromPaywallRec=false#Sec9
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-019-0516-6
The covariates included in the GWAS are insufficient, especially since proteomics aging has been shown to be non-linear. I suggest adjusting for the effects of age, sex, age-squared, age-sex interaction, age-squared-sex interaction, and the top 40 genetic PCs, as well as blood pressure, BMI, etc. In addition, the authors should run the GWAS using a mixed linear model instead to better combat aging population stratification. The Manhattan and QQ plots are missing, which is critical to check the quality of the GWAS.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This submitted manuscript is an interesting work that mainly explores the interplay between aging and disease, via computational analyses on genetic variants, genes and proteins in a tissue-specific manner as well as causal inference. Nonetheless, I have the following major concerns before any further evaluation of the scientific significance as well as the fidelity of methods and results.
(1) Lack of validation or replication procedures in the study design.
All results, including the proteomics imputation for aging rates, then GWAS and PRS, as well as the MR analysis and thereafter, were all discoveries without replication. The authors need to include at least one independent dataset to demonstrate that one or multiple parts of their results, e.g., aging-disease associations, GWAS or causal inference results, can be replicated.
For the replication data, please consider biobank or atlas data other than UKB, e.g., HuBMAP, All of Us, or MVP. Or alternatively, consider using tissue or disease-specific datasets for replicating specific result of interests, e.g., KPMP for kidney, PsychENCODE for brain, etc.
(2) Inadequate information disclosed for methods.
Not enough details were described for key approaches, especially the training of model that imputes age using protein-marker data. Why a local regression between the imputed age and chronological age via lowess function estimation will reveal the true population mean? Details as such, even if referenced from literature, are unclear to most people unless appropriately addressed. Based on the current level of disclosure, it is difficult for readers to understand or trust the methods.
In addition, please avoid using computer code-like phrase (i.e., those with an underline, e.g., Line 389-391) in the main text. If the authors feel necessary to include computer codes for the purpose of result reproducibility, please do it within the supplements as a technical protocol.
(3) Inappropriate arguments.
The authors calculated the genetic correlation between the aging statuses of different tissues, and argued that the aging among these tissues was heterogeneous… However, as shown by Figure 3C, heritability of aging in all tissues were low or merely moderate. By my experience, this level of heritability is expected; in this situation, I do not think it is fair to interpret the low genetic correlation here as evidence to the aging heterogeneity, since the heritability itself is low in overall.
Aging is a very complex trait that only a small (or moderate) proportion is genetically determined in each tissue; heterogeneity is true, whereas it is not because of genetic correlation but many contributing environmental factors.
(4) Exon annotation for prioritizing SNPs from the GWAS result is problematic.
Why did the authors use exon SNP annotation as an additional means of prioritizing the significant SNPs in GWAS? To my understanding, the only plausible reason seems to be that exons determine the protein sequence and structure, and thus if any nucleotide substitution in the exons, there will likely to be proteomic changes. However, for purpose of gene prioritization, I do not think the authors should limit the SNPs on exonic regions, although the aging traits were imputed from proteomics. Furthermore, exonic SNPs only constitute 12% of all SNPs in the genome and they are not necessarily non-synonymous.
To this end, I would encourage the authors to include intronic SNPs in the vicinity of splice junction sites. These SNPs may alter splicing and thus change the protein structure as well. In addition, please use professional bioinformatics tools or databases to evaluate the regulatory functionality of SNPs rather than using the exon annotation that is too broad and inaccurate.
Here below I list a few tools or databases for SNP function evaluation
• HGMD, ClinVar
• RegulomeDB, HeploReg (TRANSFAC, JASPAR)
• CADD, DANN, FATHMM-MKL, etc.
• ExonImpact, regSNPs-splicing, regSNPs-intron
Please update this part and also any following parts of the analyses. See if any improvements over the current results and statistical significance.
In addition to the major comments above, I also have a number of minor questions as following below. Please also address them.
(a) Figure 1, e.g., the bottom panel, may not be necessary.
(b) Figure 2A would be better if changing another way of presenting. Showing only SD increase of delta age is not informative, as people may care more about statistical significance. Consider a volcano plot-like scheme.
(c) Row labels in Figure 2D have shifted aberrantly.
(d) Figure 4D is not informative as only showing the location. Try to show direction of effects.
(e) Had the statistical results of aging status with respect to ABO (Figure 4E-4I) been adjusted for any covariates? If so say so; and if not, please consider all possible covariates and re-perform the analysis.
(f) Please use uniform scale (e.g., -4 to 6) for the y-axis in Figure 4E-4I.
(g) Line 280, typo. “Figure 6A” should be “6B”.
(h) Line 107, inappropriate argument. Rigorously, when a non-significant result, e.g., p-value > 0.05, is derived from some statistics between A and B, we can only say that the current data do not support a significant correlation between them. Whereas this should not be interpreted as A and B have no correlation at all. First, the delta age may not be the best measure of aging; second, the statistical estimation here was based on up to about 50,000 participants, it may be good enough, but we never know before seriously implementing a power analysis. Please keep all discussion scientifically rigorous throughout the paper.
(i) Line 217-218, inappropriate argument. To my understanding, the genotype-based analysis of ABO is based on the GWAS. Thus, there should not be arguments like “Consistent with the GWAS results…”.

Overall, I appreciate the authors’ diligent efforts in attempt to resolve the issues in this revision. However, as I evaluated, the issues were partially resolved, not entirely. The remaining issues are still critical. Thus, I do not think this manuscript has been in a good shape for publication unless the remaining issues were seriously taken into consideration.
Here below I provide my further comments and questions regarding these issues that still remained in the revised manuscript:
1. “Validation of the aging-disease associations”.
The process of model re-training was possibly erroneous. This is because the Elastic net method was involved in the original modeling (using the UKB data). Thus, certain proteins were ought to be selected as features in this step. The correct way of re-training models using other (independent) datasets or cohorts should be fixing on the originally selected features; in specific:
1) If those selected features also exist in the replication cohort, just use them per se with the exact pre-computed coefficients (in UKB) to impute the aging status (i.e., delta age). In this case, the model does not need and should not be re-trained.
2) If those selected features largely (but partially) exist in the other cohort, e.g., only a few missing, the prediction model should be re-trained based on the existing features only. This process usually will slightly adjust the coefficient values.
3) If those features rarely or do not show in the other cohort, you will need to discard this organ (or tissue) aging model as it is technically non-replicable. In this case, you also need to adjust the number of hypotheses accordingly if doing any multiple-hypothesis testing for the modeling results.
Such information was not reflected in either the response letter or the currently revised manuscript. To my understanding, the authors re-trained the models de novo in the replication cohorts and thus, this was not a rigorous replication. The results broadly indicated certain organs indeed associate with specific disease (risk), however, nothing to do with the validity of the (original) prediction model established upon the UKB data.
Suggestion: please follow the standard way of model result replication, as well as provide information about which specific proteins were selected as predictive features with their coefficients.
2. “Validation of GWAS result”

Biological aging refers to the gradual and cumulative changes in the biological functions of an organism as time advances1. These changes lead to a decline in physiological capabilities and an increase in disease susceptibility2,3. Investigating the underlying mechanisms of biological aging can enhance our comprehension of the processes contributing to aging-related diseases, thereby informing the development of potential therapeutic interventions.

Most of studies on biological aging focus on whole-body aging indicators, such as healthspan4, lifespan5,6 and longevity7. ### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors constructed models to predict organ-specific aging using proteomics data, and conducted a thorough investigation searching for genetic determinants of organ-specific aging in large populations. Extensive functional annotations were performed to explore effector genes of the identified loci. They also construct polygenic risk scores to assess associations with aging-related diseases for clinical implications. This study is well designed and provides very interesting results of genetic architectures for organ aging, which provide new insights into the understanding of the aging process and facilitate the discovery of anti-aging interventions. The methodology are sound to support the conclusions. The manuscript is well-written. Overall, this is a very nice piece of work, which deserves to be published. I have only a few minor points to potentially improve this work.
Comments:
1. The authors looked up whether the significant loci associated with corresponding organ-associated phenotypes in previous GWAS studies. It would be better to check the previous association results for phenotypes related to other organs, since "no organ system is an island".
2. When comparing with previous GWASs, the authors should present the results of overlapping findings.
3. Methods: The authors should provide the weights of proteins in each model to help readers understand the importance or contribution of each protein in the model’s predictions.
4. Specify the method used to assess the relationship between delta ages and diseases, which should be explicitly described in the text.
5. The authors should make the GWAS summary data publicly available.
6. In line 277, "supplementary Table 17" should be corrected to "supplementary Table 16".
7. The X-axis title is missing in Figure 5A.

### Reviewer 2

Zhu and colleagues used Olink plasma proteomics data from the UK Biobank to study the genetic architecture of the multi-organ proteomics age derived from machine learning models. Proteomics age has been an increasingly used biomarker in aging research. The authors used three different machine-learning models to derive the organ-specific age. Then, they used the Z-scores aging biomarkers as phenotypes to run a GWAS and several post-GWAS analyses. The authors made a great effort to analyze the data extensively. The topic is needed in a timely manner and may provide additional insights on previous research endeavors. However, the rigor and interpretation of these results need to be further scrutinized. Below are some of my concerns and comments.
1) Writing: Overall, the writing and flow of the current paper need improvement. Especially for the Abstract, the main messages are obscure, and it seems more like a Method section, not a highlight of the critical findings in this study. For example, the authors state: "Furthermore, we construct polygenic risk scores to assess their association with aging-related diseases. Subsequent Mendelian randomization analysis revealed the potential causal effects of organ aging on disease risk status". I don't think these are the main messages. Instead, they are the specific methods and analyses the authors used in this study. Similarly, for the rest of the manuscript, a clear flow should guide the organization of the writing, including the intuition for the genetic analyses you chose to run.
2) ML model for age prediction: Regarding the age prediction model, the authors should carefully scrutinize the model's overfitting/generalizability with the ML models you employed on the proteomics data. In the previous papers (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06802-1; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03164-7), the authors found evident model overfitting and used feature selection or regularization terms to battle this phenomenon. In the current writing, the author only showed the Pearson's r between the predicted age and chronological age in Supplementary eFigure S2 (not sure whether this is for test data and the training or the entire population). The authors should report Pearson's r and other loss metrics for the training/validation/test results to show no severe overfitting. In S Fig. 3, the authors associated the chronological age with the delta age and showed no significant associations. This is very surprising, as age bias (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2213158223000086) is very common in any age prediction model. In addition, why did the author use logistic regression to associate two quantitative variables?
3) Genetics: For GWAS, the QC'ed number of valid SNPs (13206758) is much larger than that of the previous GWAS, using imputed data from the UK Biobank. Can authors state the discrepancy?
See some references from previous UKBB GWAS:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0571-7#Sec8
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17368-1?fromPaywallRec=false#Sec9
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-019-0516-6
The covariates included in the GWAS are insufficient, especially since proteomics aging has been shown to be non-linear. I suggest adjusting for the effects of age, sex, age-squared, age-sex interaction, age-squared-sex interaction, and the top 40 genetic PCs, as well as blood pressure, BMI, etc. In addition, the authors should run the GWAS using a mixed linear model instead to better combat aging population stratification. The Manhattan and QQ plots are missing, which is critical to check the quality of the GWAS.

### Reviewer 3

This submitted manuscript is an interesting work that mainly explores the interplay between aging and disease, via computational analyses on genetic variants, genes and proteins in a tissue-specific manner as well as causal inference. Nonetheless, I have the following major concerns before any further evaluation of the scientific significance as well as the fidelity of methods and results.
(1) Lack of validation or replication procedures in the study design.
All results, including the proteomics imputation for aging rates, then GWAS and PRS, as well as the MR analysis and thereafter, were all discoveries without replication. The authors need to include at least one independent dataset to demonstrate that one or multiple parts of their results, e.g., aging-disease associations, GWAS or causal inference results, can be replicated.
For the replication data, please consider biobank or atlas data other than UKB, e.g., HuBMAP, All of Us, or MVP. Or alternatively, consider using tissue or disease-specific datasets for replicating specific result of interests, e.g., KPMP for kidney, PsychENCODE for brain, etc.
(2) Inadequate information disclosed for methods.
Not enough details were described for key approaches, especially the training of model that imputes age using protein-marker data. Why a local regression between the imputed age and chronological age via lowess function estimation will reveal the true population mean? Details as such, even if referenced from literature, are unclear to most people unless appropriately addressed. Based on the current level of disclosure, it is difficult for readers to understand or trust the methods.
In addition, please avoid using computer code-like phrase (i.e., those with an underline, e.g., Line 389-391) in the main text. If the authors feel necessary to include computer codes for the purpose of result reproducibility, please do it within the supplements as a technical protocol.
(3) Inappropriate arguments.
The authors calculated the genetic correlation between the aging statuses of different tissues, and argued that the aging among these tissues was heterogeneous… However, as shown by Figure 3C, heritability of aging in all tissues were low or merely moderate. By my experience, this level of heritability is expected; in this situation, I do not think it is fair to interpret the low genetic correlation here as evidence to the aging heterogeneity, since the heritability itself is low in overall.
Aging is a very complex trait that only a small (or moderate) proportion is genetically determined in each tissue; heterogeneity is true, whereas it is not because of genetic correlation but many contributing environmental factors.
(4) Exon annotation for prioritizing SNPs from the GWAS result is problematic.
Why did the authors use exon SNP annotation as an additional means of prioritizing the significant SNPs in GWAS? To my understanding, the only plausible reason seems to be that exons determine the protein sequence and structure, and thus if any nucleotide substitution in the exons, there will likely to be proteomic changes. However, for purpose of gene prioritization, I do not think the authors should limit the SNPs on exonic regions, although the aging traits were imputed from proteomics. Furthermore, exonic SNPs only constitute 12% of all SNPs in the genome and they are not necessarily non-synonymous.
To this end, I would encourage the authors to include intronic SNPs in the vicinity of splice junction sites. These SNPs may alter splicing and thus change the protein structure as well. In addition, please use professional bioinformatics tools or databases to evaluate the regulatory functionality of SNPs rather than using the exon annotation that is too broad and inaccurate.
Here below I list a few tools or databases for SNP function evaluation
• HGMD, ClinVar
• RegulomeDB, HeploReg (TRANSFAC, JASPAR)
• CADD, DANN, FATHMM-MKL, etc.
• ExonImpact, regSNPs-splicing, regSNPs-intron
Please update this part and also any following parts of the analyses. See if any improvements over the current results and statistical significance.
In addition to the major comments above, I also have a number of minor questions as following below. Please also address them.
(a) Figure 1, e.g., the bottom panel, may not be necessary.
(b) Figure 2A would be better if changing another way of presenting. Showing only SD increase of delta age is not informative, as people may care more about statistical significance. Consider a volcano plot-like scheme.
(c) Row labels in Figure 2D have shifted aberrantly.
(d) Figure 4D is not informative as only showing the location. Try to show direction of effects.
(e) Had the statistical results of aging status with respect to ABO (Figure 4E-4I) been adjusted for any covariates? If so say so; and if not, please consider all possible covariates and re-perform the analysis.
(f) Please use uniform scale (e.g., -4 to 6) for the y-axis in Figure 4E-4I.
(g) Line 280, typo. “Figure 6A” should be “6B”.
(h) Line 107, inappropriate argument. Rigorously, when a non-significant result, e.g., p-value > 0.05, is derived from some statistics between A and B, we can only say that the current data do not support a significant correlation between them. Whereas this should not be interpreted as A and B have no correlation at all. First, the delta age may not be the best measure of aging; second, the statistical estimation here was based on up to about 50,000 participants, it may be good enough, but we never know before seriously implementing a power analysis. Please keep all discussion scientifically rigorous throughout the paper.
(i) Line 217-218, inappropriate argument. To my understanding, the genotype-based analysis of ABO is based on the GWAS. Thus, there should not be arguments like “Consistent with the GWAS results…”.

## Paper

## Abstract

Organ-specific plasma protein signatures identified via proteomic profiling could be used to quantitatively track organ aging. However, the genetic determinants and molecular mechanisms underlying the organ-specific aging process remain poorly characterized. Here we integrated large-scale plasma proteomic and genomic data from 51,936 UK Biobank participants to uncover the genetic architectures underlying aging across 13 organs. We identified 119 genetic loci associated with organ aging, including 27 shared across multiple organs, and prioritized 554 risk genes involved in organ-relevant biological pathways, such as T cell–mediated immunity in immune aging. Causal inference analyses indicated that accelerated heart and muscle aging increase the risk of heart failure, whereas kidney aging contributes to hypertension. Moreover, smoking initiation was positively linked to the aging of the lung, intestine, kidney, and stomach. These findings establish a genetic foundation for understanding organ-specific aging and provide insights for promoting healthy longevity.

## Introduction

Biological aging refers to the gradual and cumulative changes in the biological functions of an organism as time advances1. These changes lead to a decline in physiological capabilities and an increase in disease susceptibility2,3. Investigating the underlying mechanisms of biological aging can enhance our comprehension of the processes contributing to aging-related diseases, thereby informing the development of potential therapeutic interventions.

Most of studies on biological aging focus on whole-body aging indicators, such as healthspan4, lifespan5,6 and longevity7. Given the distinct characteristics of various organs, organ aging, which refers to the biological aging specific to particular organ systems, has increasingly become a research hotspot8–10. Several methods have been established for assessing organ aging. For example, some studies11,12 used MRI-based brain volume and functional connectivity measurements to measure brain aging, but MRI measurements are costly and do not provide molecular insights. Some other studies have used clinical chemistry markers to measure organ aging8,13,14. However, many of these markers have low organ specificity, making them difficult to interpret for organ-specific aging. Moreover, suitable and easily measurable clinical chemistry markers are not yet available for some organs (e.g., intestine and stomach). Therefore, we need to find other indicators for organ aging.

Proteins are the final products of gene expression and the principal functional constituents of cellular and biological processes. Moreover, most drug targets and biomarkers are proteins15,16. In clinical practice, certain plasma proteins have been used to noninvasively evaluate the health status of specific organs, such as alanine transaminase for liver damage17,18. Therefore, finding organ-specific proteins in plasma could track human organ aging. Indeed, recent studies successfully used plasma proteomics data to predict organ aging9,19,20. However, these studies primarily focused on identifying correlations between aging and other phenotypes, without delving into the underlying genetic determinants of organ aging. Moreover, causal associations between organ aging and diseases were not explored.

In this study, using plasma proteomics data from the UK Biobank PharmaProteomics Project (UKB-PPP)21, we trained models to predict organ aging for 13 human organs. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) was then performed to pinpoint the genomic loci associated with organ aging. Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was further used to explore the causal relationship between aging-related diseases, modifiable lifestyle factors and organ aging. Our results could enhance the comprehension of the genetic basis of organ aging and highlighted the causal relationship between organ aging and other traits.

### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors constructed models to predict organ-specific aging using proteomics data, and conducted a thorough investigation searching for genetic determinants of organ-specific aging in large populations. ### Reviewer 2

Zhu and colleagues used Olink plasma proteomics data from the UK Biobank to study the genetic architecture of the multi-organ proteomics age derived from machine learning models. Proteomics age has been an increasingly used biomarker in aging research. The authors used three different machine-learning models to derive the organ-specific age. Then, they used the Z-scores aging biomarkers as phenotypes to run a GWAS and several post-GWAS analyses. The authors made a great effort to analyze the data extensively. The topic is needed in a timely manner and may provide additional insights on previous research endeavors. However, the rigor and interpretation of these results need to be further scrutinized. Below are some of my concerns and comments.
1) Writing: Overall, the writing and flow of the current paper need improvement. Especially for the Abstract, the main messages are obscure, and it seems more like a Method section, not a highlight of the critical findings in this study. For example, the authors state: "Furthermore, we construct polygenic risk scores to assess their association with aging-related diseases. Subsequent Mendelian randomization analysis revealed the potential causal effects of organ aging on disease risk status". I don't think these are the main messages. Instead, they are the specific methods and analyses the authors used in this study. Similarly, for the rest of the manuscript, a clear flow should guide the organization of the writing, including the intuition for the genetic analyses you chose to run.
2) ML model for age prediction: Regarding the age prediction model, the authors should carefully scrutinize the model's overfitting/generalizability with the ML models you employed on the proteomics data. In the previous papers (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06802-1; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03164-7), the authors found evident model overfitting and used feature selection or regularization terms to battle this phenomenon. The authors should report Pearson's r and other loss metrics for the training/validation/test results to show no severe overfitting. In S Fig. 3, the authors associated the chronological age with the delta age and showed no significant associations. This is very surprising, as age bias (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2213158223000086) is very common in any age prediction model. In addition, why did the author use logistic regression to associate two quantitative variables?

### Reviewer 3

This submitted manuscript is an interesting work that mainly explores the interplay between aging and disease, via computational analyses on genetic variants, genes and proteins in a tissue-specific manner as well as causal inference. Nonetheless, I have the following major concerns before any further evaluation of the scientific significance as well as the fidelity of methods and results.
(1) Lack of validation or replication procedures in the study design.
All results, including the proteomics imputation for aging rates, then GWAS and PRS, as well as the MR analysis and thereafter, were all discoveries without replication. The authors need to include at least one independent dataset to demonstrate that one or multiple parts of their results, e.g., aging-disease associations, GWAS or causal inference results, can be replicated.
For the replication data, please consider biobank or atlas data other than UKB, e.g., HuBMAP, All of Us, or MVP. Or alternatively, consider using tissue or disease-specific datasets for replicating specific result of interests, e.g., KPMP for kidney, PsychENCODE for brain, etc.
(2) Inadequate information disclosed for methods.
Not enough details were described for key approaches, especially the training of model that imputes age using protein-marker data. Why a local regression between the imputed age and chronological age via lowess function estimation will reveal the true population mean? Details as such, even if referenced from literature, are unclear to most people unless appropriately addressed. Based on the current level of disclosure, it is difficult for readers to understand or trust the methods.
In addition, please avoid using computer code-like phrase (i.e., those with an underline, e.g., Line 389-391) in the main text. If the authors feel necessary to include computer codes for the purpose of result reproducibility, please do it within the supplements as a technical protocol.
(3) Inappropriate arguments.
The authors calculated the genetic correlation between the aging statuses of different tissues, and argued that the aging among these tissues was heterogeneous… However, as shown by Figure 3C, heritability of aging in all tissues were low or merely moderate. By my experience, this level of heritability is expected; in this situation, I do not think it is fair to interpret the low genetic correlation here as evidence to the aging heterogeneity, since the heritability itself is low in overall.
Aging is a very complex trait that only a small (or moderate) proportion is genetically determined in each tissue; heterogeneity is true, whereas it is not because of genetic correlation but many contributing environmental factors.
(4) Exon annotation for prioritizing SNPs from the GWAS result is problematic.
Why did the authors use exon SNP annotation as an additional means of prioritizing the significant SNPs in GWAS? To my understanding, the only plausible reason seems to be that exons determine the protein sequence and structure, and thus if any nucleotide substitution in the exons, there will likely to be proteomic changes. However, for purpose of gene prioritization, I do not think the authors should limit the SNPs on exonic regions, although the aging traits were imputed from proteomics. Furthermore, exonic SNPs only constitute 12% of all SNPs in the genome and they are not necessarily non-synonymous.
To this end, I would encourage the authors to include intronic SNPs in the vicinity of splice junction sites. These SNPs may alter splicing and thus change the protein structure as well. In addition, please use professional bioinformatics tools or databases to evaluate the regulatory functionality of SNPs rather than using the exon annotation that is too broad and inaccurate.

• HGMD, ClinVar

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors constructed models to predict organ-specific aging using proteomics data, and conducted a thorough investigation searching for genetic determinants of organ-specific aging in large populations. Extensive functional annotations were performed to explore effector genes of the identified loci. They also construct polygenic risk scores to assess associations with aging-related diseases for clinical implications. This study is well designed and provides very interesting results of genetic architectures for organ aging, which provide new insights into the understanding of the aging process and facilitate the discovery of anti-aging interventions. The methodology are sound to support the conclusions. The manuscript is well-written. Overall, this is a very nice piece of work, which deserves to be published. I have only a few minor points to potentially improve this work.
Comments:
1. The authors looked up whether the significant loci associated with corresponding organ-associated phenotypes in previous GWAS studies. It would be better to check the previous association results for phenotypes related to other organs, since "no organ system is an island".
2. When comparing with previous GWASs, the authors should present the results of overlapping findings.
3. Methods: The authors should provide the weights of proteins in each model to help readers understand the importance or contribution of each protein in the model’s predictions.
4. Specify the method used to assess the relationship between delta ages and diseases, which should be explicitly described in the text.
5. The authors should make the GWAS summary data publicly available.
6. In line 277, "supplementary Table 17" should be corrected to "supplementary Table 16".
7. The X-axis title is missing in Figure 5A.

### Reviewer 2

Zhu and colleagues used Olink plasma proteomics data from the UK Biobank to study the genetic architecture of the multi-organ proteomics age derived from machine learning models. Proteomics age has been an increasingly used biomarker in aging research. The authors used three different machine-learning models to derive the organ-specific age. Then, they used the Z-scores aging biomarkers as phenotypes to run a GWAS and several post-GWAS analyses. The authors made a great effort to analyze the data extensively. The topic is needed in a timely manner and may provide additional insights on previous research endeavors. However, the rigor and interpretation of these results need to be further scrutinized. Below are some of my concerns and comments.
1) Writing: Overall, the writing and flow of the current paper need improvement. Especially for the Abstract, the main messages are obscure, and it seems more like a Method section, not a highlight of the critical findings in this study. For example, the authors state: "Furthermore, we construct polygenic risk scores to assess their association with aging-related diseases. Subsequent Mendelian randomization analysis revealed the potential causal effects of organ aging on disease risk status". I don't think these are the main messages. Instead, they are the specific methods and analyses the authors used in this study. Similarly, for the rest of the manuscript, a clear flow should guide the organization of the writing, including the intuition for the genetic analyses you chose to run.
2) ML model for age prediction: Regarding the age prediction model, the authors should carefully scrutinize the model's overfitting/generalizability with the ML models you employed on the proteomics data. In the previous papers (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06802-1; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03164-7), the authors found evident model overfitting and used feature selection or regularization terms to battle this phenomenon. In the current writing, the author only showed the Pearson's r between the predicted age and chronological age in Supplementary eFigure S2 (not sure whether this is for test data and the training or the entire population). The authors should report Pearson's r and other loss metrics for the training/validation/test results to show no severe overfitting. In S Fig. 3, the authors associated the chronological age with the delta age and showed no significant associations. This is very surprising, as age bias (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2213158223000086) is very common in any age prediction model. In addition, why did the author use logistic regression to associate two quantitative variables?
3) Genetics: For GWAS, the QC'ed number of valid SNPs (13206758) is much larger than that of the previous GWAS, using imputed data from the UK Biobank. Can authors state the discrepancy?
See some references from previous UKBB GWAS:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0571-7#Sec8

The covariates included in the GWAS are insufficient, especially since proteomics aging has been shown to be non-linear. I suggest adjusting for the effects of age, sex, age-squared, age-sex interaction, age-squared-sex interaction, and the top 40 genetic PCs, as well as blood pressure, BMI, etc. In addition, the authors should run the GWAS using a mixed linear model instead to better combat aging population stratification. ### Reviewer 3

This submitted manuscript is an interesting work that mainly explores the interplay between aging and disease, via computational analyses on genetic variants, genes and proteins in a tissue-specific manner as well as causal inference. Nonetheless, I have the following major concerns before any further evaluation of the scientific significance as well as the fidelity of methods and results.
(1) Lack of validation or replication procedures in the study design.
All results, including the proteomics imputation for aging rates, then GWAS and PRS, as well as the MR analysis and thereafter, were all discoveries without replication. The authors need to include at least one independent dataset to demonstrate that one or multiple parts of their results, e.g., aging-disease associations, GWAS or causal inference results, can be replicated.
For the replication data, please consider biobank or atlas data other than UKB, e.g., HuBMAP, All of Us, or MVP. Or alternatively, consider using tissue or disease-specific datasets for replicating specific result of interests, e.g., KPMP for kidney, PsychENCODE for brain, etc.
(2) Inadequate information disclosed for methods.
Not enough details were described for key approaches, especially the training of model that imputes age using protein-marker data. Why a local regression between the imputed age and chronological age via lowess function estimation will reveal the true population mean? Details as such, even if referenced from literature, are unclear to most people unless appropriately addressed. Based on the current level of disclosure, it is difficult for readers to understand or trust the methods.
In addition, please avoid using computer code-like phrase (i.e., those with an underline, e.g., Line 389-391) in the main text. If the authors feel necessary to include computer codes for the purpose of result reproducibility, please do it within the supplements as a technical protocol.
(3) Inappropriate arguments.
The authors calculated the genetic correlation between the aging statuses of different tissues, and argued that the aging among these tissues was heterogeneous… However, as shown by Figure 3C, heritability of aging in all tissues were low or merely moderate. By my experience, this level of heritability is expected; in this situation, I do not think it is fair to interpret the low genetic correlation here as evidence to the aging heterogeneity, since the heritability itself is low in overall.
Aging is a very complex trait that only a small (or moderate) proportion is genetically determined in each tissue; heterogeneity is true, whereas it is not because of genetic correlation but many contributing environmental factors.
(4) Exon annotation for prioritizing SNPs from the GWAS result is problematic.
Why did the authors use exon SNP annotation as an additional means of prioritizing the significant SNPs in GWAS? To my understanding, the only plausible reason seems to be that exons determine the protein sequence and structure, and thus if any nucleotide substitution in the exons, there will likely to be proteomic changes. However, for purpose of gene prioritization, I do not think the authors should limit the SNPs on exonic regions, although the aging traits were imputed from proteomics. Furthermore, exonic SNPs only constitute 12% of all SNPs in the genome and they are not necessarily non-synonymous.
To this end, I would encourage the authors to include intronic SNPs in the vicinity of splice junction sites. These SNPs may alter splicing and thus change the protein structure as well. In addition, please use professional bioinformatics tools or databases to evaluate the regulatory functionality of SNPs rather than using the exon annotation that is too broad and inaccurate.
Here below I list a few tools or databases for SNP function evaluation
• HGMD, ClinVar
• RegulomeDB, HeploReg (TRANSFAC, JASPAR)
• CADD, DANN, FATHMM-MKL, etc.
• ExonImpact, regSNPs-splicing, regSNPs-intron
Please update this part and also any following parts of the analyses. See if any improvements over the current results and statistical significance.
In addition to the major comments above, I also have a number of minor questions as following below. Please also address them.
(a) Figure 1, e.g., the bottom panel, may not be necessary.
(b) Figure 2A would be better if changing another way of presenting. Showing only SD increase of delta age is not informative, as people may care more about statistical significance. Consider a volcano plot-like scheme.
(c) Row labels in Figure 2D have shifted aberrantly.
(d) Figure 4D is not informative as only showing the location. Try to show direction of effects.
(e) Had the statistical results of aging status with respect to ABO (Figure 4E-4I) been adjusted for any covariates? If so say so; and if not, please consider all possible covariates and re-perform the analysis.
(f) Please use uniform scale (e.g., -4 to 6) for the y-axis in Figure 4E-4I.
(g) Line 280, typo. “Figure 6A” should be “6B”.
(h) Line 107, inappropriate argument. Rigorously, when a non-significant result, e.g., p-value > 0.05, is derived from some statistics between A and B, we can only say that the current data do not support a significant correlation between them. Whereas this should not be interpreted as A and B have no correlation at all. First, the delta age may not be the best measure of aging; second, the statistical estimation here was based on up to about 50,000 participants, it may be good enough, but we never know before seriously implementing a power analysis. Please keep all discussion scientifically rigorous throughout the paper.
(i) Line 217-218, inappropriate argument. To my understanding, the genotype-based analysis of ABO is based on the GWAS. Thus, there should not be arguments like “Consistent with the GWAS results…”.
